title: Interfacial Response of Bacterial Community Vertical Shifts in the Ice‐Water‐Sediment Vertical Sedimentary Chain of Frozen Lake Dali
content:
Abstract

High-latitude lakes are ecologically important, particularly during ice-covered periods, when three distinct media (ice, water, and sediment) and two critical interfaces, the ice-water interface (IWI) and sediment-water interface (SWI), are formed. Using 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing, we investigated the structural characteristics of bacterial communities across these media and interfaces in Lake Dali, northern China. Along the ice-water-sediment chain, the relative abundances of Proteobacteria, Actinobacteria, and Chloroflexi varied vertically with changes in phosphorus, NH4 +-N, and pH, and these groups predominated in ice, water, and sediment, respectively. Network properties differed markedly among media. Water samples exhibited higher modularity and lower network density than ice and sediment samples. The operational taxonomic units associated with ecological network stability also differed between IWI and SWI. These findings suggest that environmental conditions and medium properties influence the importance of ecological network nodes, whereas relative abundance alone does not necessarily determine their importance. In ice and sediment, the solid-state properties of the media reduced mass transfer efficiency and increased environmental isolation among communities. Consequently, stochastic processes dominated community assembly, with drift accounting for more than 30%, although heterogeneous selection also contributed substantially. In contrast, the fluidity of water increased the contribution of deterministic processes. In the water column, homogeneous selection dominated bacterial community assembly and facilitated microbial dispersal between communities. This study sheds light on the distinctive environmental distribution patterns, ecological interactions, and community assembly mechanisms of bacterial communities in frozen lakes, thereby enhancing our understanding of microbial ecological processes across ice-water-sediment interfaces.
